title: Ship It Safely
summary: Ferncart trades fortnightly big-bang releases for a pipeline, feature flags, blue-green, canaries with automatic rollback and safe schema changes.

goals.text: Build once and promote one artifact through pipeline stages
Separate deploying code from releasing features with flags
Roll back automatically when a canary misbehaves
Change a database schema without downtime (expand/contract)

steps.title: The fortnightly release train
body: Ferncart's tests are in good shape now, but shipping is still an event. Every other Thursday night an engineer copies the new build to all four servers and restarts them.
Each release carries about 40 commits from two weeks of work. If anything goes wrong, rolling back means rebuilding the previous version by hand.

steps.title: Everything breaks at once
body: Release v42 includes a commit that reads a new config key nobody added in production. Checkout crashes on all four servers at the same moment.
Which of the 40 commits did it? It takes four hours to find the cause, revert, rebuild and redeploy. Every shopper was affected the whole time.

callout.text: Big batches make failures both more likely and harder to diagnose, and an all-at-once rollout makes them hit everyone.

steps.title: A pipeline that builds once
body: A CI/CD pipeline turns every merge into the same sequence of stages: build, test, deploy. No laptop, no manual steps.
The key rule: build once, promote the same artifact. The image tagged a3f9c1 that passed tests is byte-for-byte what reaches production; only configuration changes per environment.
Because every artifact is kept, rolling back is just deploying the previous one again: minutes, not hours.

steps.title: Deploy is not release
body: With feature flags, new code ships switched off: if (flags.on("new-checkout", user)). Deploying becomes boring; releasing is a separate, reversible decision.
The team turns the new checkout on for staff, then 5% of shoppers, then everyone. If it misbehaves, flipping the flag off takes seconds and needs no deploy.

callout.text: Flags are debt: give each one an owner and delete it once the rollout is done.

changes: ~ Servers run v43 with the feature dark
~ 5% of shoppers see the new checkout

steps.title: Blue-green: two fleets and a switch
body: In a blue-green deployment there are two identical fleets. The new version goes to the idle one, gets smoke-tested, and then the load balancer flips all traffic over at once.

Rollback is flipping back, which takes seconds. The costs: double the servers during a release, and every shopper moves at the same instant, so a bug that only shows under real load still hits everyone.
changes: ~ Fleet split into blue (v43) and green (v44)
~ Load balancer now sends all traffic to green
~ Blue kept warm for instant rollback

steps.title: Canary: let a few go first
body: A canary release puts the new version on one server and sends it a small slice of traffic (here about 5%).

An automated canary judge compares the canary with a baseline server running the old version over the same minutes: error rate, p95 latency, saturation. Comparing against the same moment avoids blaming the canary for a normal evening peak.
If the numbers stay close for 15 minutes, the rollout widens step by step: 5% → 25% → 100%.
changes: ~ One server runs v45 as the canary
+ Canary judge watches canary vs baseline

steps.title: The canary coughs
body: Six minutes in, v45's error rate climbs to 4.1% while the baseline sits at 0.3%. A missing database index makes one checkout query time out under real data.
No human is watching a dashboard at that moment, and none needs to: the judge's thresholds were agreed in advance, so it fires the rollback on its own.

steps.title: Automatic rollback
body: The canary goes back to v44 within 90 seconds and the pipeline blocks v45 from going any further. About 5% of shoppers saw errors for a minute and a half.
Compare that with the v42 release: every shopper, for four hours. Same kind of bug, very different blast radius.

callout.text: You cannot stop every bad change from shipping. You can decide how many people it touches and for how long.

steps.title: Code rolls back. Data doesn't.
body: During any canary or blue-green release, old and new code run at the same time against one database. Renaming a column in one go breaks whichever version expects the old name, and you cannot roll that back by redeploying.
So schema changes follow expand/contract: first add the new shape alongside the old, move code and data over in separate deploys, and remove the old shape only once nothing uses it.
changes: ~ Schema holds zip and postal_code together

card.title: Expand → contract
lines: 5 contract: stop writing zip, DROP it
= every step can be rolled back alone

steps.title: Smaller, more often, safer
body: Ferncart now ships about 20 times a day, two commits at a time. That sounds riskier, but it is the opposite: a small change is easy to review, easy to judge on a canary, and obvious to revert.
The four numbers in the HUD are the classic delivery health metrics: how often you deploy, how long a commit takes to reach users, how often a deploy fails, and how fast you recover.

steps.title: Ship it safely
body:
• Pipeline: build once, promote the same artifact through every stage.
  • Feature flags: deploy dark, release gradually, kill switch in seconds.
  • Blue-green: instant switch and rollback, but everyone moves at once.
  • Canary: a small slice first, judged automatically against a baseline, rolled back without a human.
  • Expand/contract: every schema change must work for old and new code at once.
  • Small, frequent deploys shrink both risk and recovery time.
